evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Prescribing statins may protect against infection with RNA viruses such as members of family Flaviviridae, including dengue virus, Zika virus, and West Nile virus.
source: and that prescribing statins may protect against infection with RNA viruses such as members of family Flaviviridae, including dengue virus, Zika virus, and West Nile virus (Gower and Graham, 2001; Osuna-Ramos et al., 2018; Whitehorn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Risedronic acid acts on the enzyme farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase.
source: The involvement of the cholesterol/ubiquinone pathway is further confirmed by the fact that risedronic acid, a drug acting on the enzyme farnesyl pyrophoshate synthase (Tsoumpra et al., 2015; Figure 2)
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase catalyzes the production of FPP from which the cholesterol and the ubiquinone synthesis pathways split.
source: which catalyzes the production of FPP from which the cholesterol and the ubiquinone synthesis pathways split (Buhaescu and Izzedine, 2007)
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may hijack the cholesterol synthesis pathway, possibly to boost production of the cellular cholesterol it needs as an RNA virus.
source: Taken together, our findings lend (albeit indirect) support to the possibility that SARS-CoV-2 hijacks the cholesterol synthesis pathway, possibly to boost production of the cellular cholesterol it needs as an RNA virus.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study findings.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may tilt the mevalonate pathway toward cholesterol synthesis and away from ubiquinone synthesis.
source: The fact that ubiquinone protects against severe disease suggests that SARS-CoV-2 may tilt the mevalonate pathway toward cholesterol synthesis and away from ubiquinone synthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study findings.

claim: A pathway imbalance tilting toward cholesterol and away from ubiquinone would ultimately result in deficiency of ubiquinone that could lead to cell death unless counteracted by ubiquinone supplementation.
source: Such a pathway imbalance would ultimately result in deficiency of ubiquinone that could lead to cell death unless counteracted by ubiquinone supplementation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study findings.

claim: The protective effect of anti-cholesterol drugs was observed mostly for rosuvastatin and in cohort 1 for pravastatin, but not for other statins.
source: It is remarkable that the protective effect of anti-cholesterol drugs was observed mostly for rosuvastatin – and in cohort 1 for pravastatin – but not for other statins.
evidence: This is an observation from the study findings.

claim: Rosuvastatin was found to significantly increase 25-OH vitamin D levels in the blood.
source: Rosuvastatin was found to significantly increase 25-OH vitamin D levels in the blood (Yavuz et al., 2009), much more than what could be observed with other statins.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Rosuvastatin increases 25-OH vitamin D levels much more than what could be observed with other statins.
source: Rosuvastatin was found to significantly increase 25-OH vitamin D levels in the blood (Yavuz et al., 2009), much more than what could be observed with other statins.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The increase in 25-OH vitamin D observed following rosuvastatin treatment could be mediated by the Niemann-Pick C1 like 1 (NPC1L1) membrane transporter that is involved in intestinal absorption of vitamin D.
source: Yavuz and Ertugrul, 2012 suggested that the increase in 25-OH vitamin D observed following rosuvastatin treatment could be mediated by the Niemann-Pick C1 like 1 (NPC1L1) membrane transporter that is involved in intestinal absorption of vitamin D.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: The NPC1L1 membrane transporter is the target of ezetimibe.
source: Interestingly, the NPC1L1 membrane transporter is also the target of ezetimibe, identified by our study to decrease significantly the hospitalization risk of COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Vitamin D deficiency has been shown to be associated with increased risk for COVID-19 in multiple studies.
source: Vitamin D deficiency has been shown to be associated with increased risk for COVID-19 in multiple studies (Israel et al., 2020; Merzon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Magnesium is needed for vitamin D activation.
source: Magnesium is needed for vitamin D activation (Uwitonze and Razzaque, 2018)
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Magnesium levels in drinking water in Israel are low, as water is produced in great part through desalination of sea water.
source: and its levels in drinking water in Israel are low, as water is produced in great part through desalination of sea water (Koren et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about water supply in Israel, supported by citation.

claim: Flecainide is an antiarrhythmic drug that blocks sodium channels in the heart and inhibits ryanodine receptor 2.
source: Another medication that was associated with decreased odds for hospitalization is flecainide, an antiarrhythmic drug that blocks sodium channels in the heart, and inhibits ryanodine receptor 2, a major regulator of sarcoplasmic release of stored calcium ions.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Ryanodine receptor 2 is a major regulator of sarcoplasmic release of stored calcium ions.
source: an antiarrhythmic drug that blocks sodium channels in the heart, and inhibits ryanodine receptor 2, a major regulator of sarcoplasmic release of stored calcium ions.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Flecainide may prevent apoptosis by release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum once the cell mitochondria cease to function.
source: It may prevent apoptosis by release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) once the cell mitochondria cease to function.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism of action.

claim: An expert review recommended that patients with arrhythmia who get COVID-19 should continue flecainide treatment if already prescribed.
source: An expert review recommended that patients with arrhythmia who get COVID-19 should continue flecainide treatment if already prescribed (Ci et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation from prior literature, supported by citation.

claim: The protective effect of flecainide observed in both cohorts is even more marked for severe patients.
source: In our study, the protective effect observed in both cohorts is even more marked for severe patients
evidence: This is an observation from the study findings.

claim: Flecainide can be given intravenously.
source: suggesting that this drug, which can be given intravenously (Antonelli et al., 2006), could be administered to patients in respiratory distress, if the protective effect is confirmed in clinical trials.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: ACE and ARB treated patients have been shown to not have an increased risk for COVID-19.
source: These results are consistent with ACE and ARBs treated patients shown to not have an increased risk for COVID-19 (Morales et al., 2021)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: There is no reason to discontinue ACE inhibitors or ARBs to decrease COVID-19 risk.
source: and there is therefore no reason to discontinue these medications to decrease COVID-19 risk.
evidence: This is a clinical inference based on the study findings and prior research.

claim: Recent EHR-based findings show a favorable association between metformin use and COVID-19 outcomes.
source: Our findings also confirm and substantially extend recent EHR-based findings about the favorable association between metformin use and COVID-19 outcomes (Bramante et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 invades neuronal cells.
source: This is consistent with SARS-CoV-2 invading neuronal cells (Iroegbu et al., 2020; Meinhardt et al., 2021; Song et al., 2021)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citations.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may spread throughout the nervous system across synapses.
source: as manifest by symptoms of loss of smell and taste, where it may spread throughout the nervous system across synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on clinical observations and prior research.

claim: Decreased neurotransmitter internalization may reduce the infectious potential of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Decreased neurotransmitter internalization may therefore reduce the infectious potential of the virus.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism to explain the protective effect of neurotransmitter-acting drugs.

claim: Items that could improve the physical barrier of the eye surface were among the top items decreasing odds of hospitalization.
source: Interestingly, items that could improve the physical barrier of the eye surface were among the top items decreasing odds of hospitalization, including eye wipes, artificial tears, and eye ointments.
evidence: This is an observation from the study findings.

claim: The protective effect for ophthalmologic barrier items was observed foremost among patients from cohort 2 in which controls are already SARS-CoV-2 positive.
source: Interestingly, the protective effect for these items was observed foremost among patients from cohort 2 in which controls are already SARS-CoV-2 positive.
evidence: This is an observation from the study findings.

claim: Ophthalmologic barrier items could not only protect against the initial risk of infection, but also reduce disease severity in patients already infected.
source: This suggests that these barrier items could not only protect against the initial risk of infection, but, notably, also reduce disease severity in patients already infected.
evidence: This is an inference from the cohort 2 findings.

claim: Autoinoculation of SARS-CoV-2 to the eyes may have a role in the virulence of SARS-CoV-2.
source: The beneficial effect observed here for many different ophthalmologic preparations raises the possibility that autoinoculation of the virus to the eyes, prevented by these items, has a role in the virulence of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study findings.

claim: Eyeglass wearers were shown previously to be at decreased risk for COVID-19 hospitalization.
source: The possibility that invasion of the central nervous system by the virus through the eyes could increase the risk of COVID-19 complications is also supported by the fact that eyeglass wearers were shown previously to be at decreased risk for COVID-19 hospitalization (Zeng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation.

claim: Invasion of the central nervous system by SARS-CoV-2 through the eyes could increase the risk of COVID-19 complications.
source: The possibility that invasion of the central nervous system by the virus through the eyes could increase the risk of COVID-19 complications is also supported by the fact that eyeglass wearers were shown previously to be at decreased risk for COVID-19 hospitalization (Zeng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by prior research.

claim: The study shows apparently protective effects for rosuvastatin, ezetimibe, ubiquinone, risedronate, vitamin D, and magnesium.
source: In conclusion, this study shows apparently protective effects for several medications and dietary supplements, such as rosuvastatin, ezetimibe, ubiquinone, risedronate, vitamin D, and magnesium.
evidence: This is a summary of the study findings.

claim: The observed protective effects of rosuvastatin, ezetimibe, ubiquinone, risedronate, vitamin D, and magnesium provide important evidence supporting their safe continuation for COVID-19 patients.
source: In the meantime, we believe that the observed protective effects of these drugs provide important evidence supporting their safe continuation for COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Clalit Health Services is the largest healthcare provider in Israel, insuring over 4.7 million members.
source: Toward this objective, we conducted a large population study in Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest healthcare provider in Israel, insuring over 4.7 million members.
evidence: This is factual information about the healthcare system.

claim: The study was approved by the CHS Institutional Review Board with a waiver of informed consent, approval number: COM-0046–20.
source: This study has been approved by the CHS Institutional Review Board (IRB) with a waiver of informed consent, approval number: COM-0046–20.
evidence: This is information about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: Patient data that could identify participants were removed prior to the statistical analyses in accordance with the protocol approved by the CHS IRB.
source: Patient data that could identify participants were removed prior to the statistical analyses in accordance with the protocol approved by the CHS IRB.
evidence: This describes the data privacy procedures.

claim: The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report.
source: The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report.
evidence: This is a statement about the independence of the research.
